notes: The tutorial does not fix the breadboard layout or GND pin; the layout was chosen so each button straddles the centre gap. The GPIO lead goes to the top-half side of the button and a GND lead goes to the bottom-half side. A pin-to-socket lead from a Pi GND pin feeds the bottom negative rail 'bn'.

GPIO numbers (4, 17, 27, 10) come from the tutorial's full code listing. They are named as GPIO ports on rpi1, along with GND. The catalogue's rpi-4b entry lists only GPIO_HEADER, so these header-pin names are an assumed extension.
Each button's GPIO is wired to one side and ground to the other side. The code uses gpiozero Button, which enables the internal pull-up, so no external resistor is needed.
The five pin-to-socket leads are four GPIO leads and one GND lead. The four pin-to-pin leads link the GND rail to each button.

The speaker's audio_in is shown plugged into the Pi's 3.5mm audio jack. The catalogue's rpi-4b has no audio-jack port, so the Pi end has no port name. The speaker's USB power is assumed to come from a Pi USB 2.0 port. The tutorial only says 'speakers or headphones'.

Pushbutton legs 1.l and 1.r are one internal side, and 2.l and 2.r are the other. Both legs of each side are placed in the breadboard as a physical button would be. Electrical wiring uses one column per side.
The software steps (pygame, sample WAV files, Thonny) are not physical parts and are not in the graph.
